first_draft.title: Alice, Bob and the Blue Marble
first_draft.text:
Alice had a best friend named Bob, and Bob was a cat. He was a fat orange cat with one white sock on his back left paw, and he could open the kitchen cupboard with his nose when he wanted a biscuit.

One rainy Tuesday, Alice sat by the window with her chin in her hands. The raindrops ran down the glass like tiny silver snakes. "I lost my blue marble," she sighed. "My lucky one. The one that goes glim, glim, glim when the light hits it."

Bob hopped up beside her and sniffed the windowsill. He sniffed the cushion. He sniffed the bottom of the toy box, which made him sneeze twice. "Prrrf! Prrrf!" he said, and Alice giggled, even though she was still sad.

They searched under the bed, behind the bookshelf, and inside Alice's wellington boots. They found a sock, half a crayon, and a very old raisin. They did not find the marble. Alice flopped onto the rug. "Maybe it rolled away forever," she said.

Bob sat very still. His ears swivelled toward the hallway. Tap, tap, tap went something small and hard across the floorboards. Bob crept after it, his tail held high like a question mark. Alice tiptoed behind him.

The sound led them to the bathroom, where the bath mat was rumpled and the cupboard door stood open a crack. Bob pushed the door with his nose. Out rolled a blue marble, bouncing once, twice, then lying still beside the cat's fluffy paw.

"Bob, you found it!" Alice cried, scooping it up. It glimmered in her palm like a little blue moon.

Bob blinked slowly, very pleased with himself, and began to wash his white sock as if it were the most important job in the world.

Alice held the marble to the lamp and watched the light dance inside it. The rain had softened to a gentle patter on the roof. She yawned a big, wide yawn.

"Thank you, Bob," she whispered.

Bob curled into a warm orange circle at the foot of her bed. The marble glowed softly on her pillow. The house grew quiet, and the rain hummed its slow, sleepy song, and both friends drifted off, side by side, into the dark.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Leo and Rocket's Backyard Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo had a map that smelled like old tea and crinkled like a potato chip bag. It was drawn in brown ink, with a big red X near the old swing set. Rocket, his scruffy brown dog, sniffed the paper with his wet black nose. Then he sneezed, a tiny, wobbly sneeze, and wagged his whole back end.

"Ahoy, first mate," Leo whispered. He tucked the map into his pocket and pulled on his yellow rain boots. The back door creaked open, and the evening air was cool and full of the smell of cut grass.

The backyard looked different in the dusk. The apple tree stood tall, its branches like twisting arms. The garden hose coiled beside the fence like a sleeping snake. Leo marched past the tomato plants, counting his steps out loud. "One, two, three, four, five!" Rocket trotted beside him, his tail swishing through the tall grass.

At step twenty, Rocket stopped. His ears shot up. He dug his front paws into the dirt, sending little clods flying. Thump, thump, thump! Something clanked underneath.

"Rocket, you found something!" Leo dropped to his knees and scooped the soil away with his hands. His fingers hit something hard and cold. It was a metal box, dented at one corner, with a rusty latch.

But the latch was stuck. Leo pulled. He pushed. He wiggled it side to side. The box would not budge. Rocket whined and pawed at the lid, and Leo felt his cheeks go hot with frustration.

"Hmm," Leo said, sitting back on his heels. He looked at the map again. In the corner, in tiny letters, were words he had missed before. Find the spade, then the sun will show the way.

Leo looked around. Leaning against the shed was a small garden trowel, its handle painted green. He grabbed it and slid the flat end under the latch. With a sharp, satisfied click, the box popped open.

Inside lay a folded paper, a shiny blue marble, and a chocolate coin wrapped in gold foil. Leo gasped. Rocket barked, a loud, happy woof that made a sleepy bird flap out of the apple tree.

Leo unfolded the paper. It was not a treasure map at all. It was a note in his grandmother's loopy handwriting. For my little pirate, it said. Hunt well, and come inside for cocoa when you are done.

Leo laughed so hard he had to hold his stomach. "Rocket, we found the best treasure of all," he said. Rocket licked his chin, and Leo decided that was true.

He tucked the marble in his pocket and the coin in his other pocket. Then he and Rocket walked slowly back toward the glowing kitchen window. The crickets had started their soft, steady song. The tree leaves rustled like whispers.

Inside, a mug of cocoa waited on the table, steaming gently. Leo climbed into his chair and wrapped both hands around the warm cup. Rocket curled up under the table with a long, contented sigh.

Outside, the moon rose slowly over the apple tree. Leo's eyelids grew heavy. The map lay folded beside his cup, and the blue marble glowed softly in the lamplight. Rocket's breathing slowed. Goodnight, backyard. Goodnight, pirate. Goodnight.

first_draft.title: Pim and the Wobbly Wings
first_draft.text:
Once upon a time, in a mossy valley, there lived a little dragon named Pim. Pim was small and green, with smoky puffs for breath and tiny wings like wet paper fans.

Every morning, the big dragons soared over the hills. Whoosh! Whoosh! Their wings made the tall grass bend and sway.

Pim stood on the edge of the cliff. Her knees wobbled. Her tail curled tight around her toes.

"Jump, Pim!" called her cousin Bramble. "The wind will hold you up!"

Pim peeked over the edge. The valley looked very far down. "I can't," she whispered. "My wings are too little."

So Pim tried a different way. She hopped onto a flat stone and flapped. Flap, flap, flap. Nothing happened but a tiny puff of smoke.

Puff! Pop! A bubble of smoke floated up and bumped her nose. Pim giggled. The bubble wobbled away over the grass.

Pim watched it drift. It rose, and rose, and then it floated gently down again.

"Bubbles don't mind being light," Pim said slowly. "Maybe I could be light, too."

She took a deep breath. She didn't jump. Instead she spread her wings wide and let the warm wind lift her, just a little, like a leaf.

Her belly tickled. Her toes lifted off the stone. Pim wobbled, then steadied, and drifted down onto the soft moss.

"Again!" said Bramble, bouncing.

Pim tried again. Up went one paw. Down went one paw. She swooped, she wobbled, and she landed with a soft thump on her bottom. Bramble laughed so hard that a tiny puff of smoke came out of his ears.

The sun slid low behind the hills. The sky turned peach and then lavender. The big dragons came home, their wings folded like sleepy umbrellas.

Pim sat on the moss beside her cousin. Her wings felt tired and warm.

"Tomorrow," she yawned, "I'll try a little higher."

Bramble curled up beside her. The grass whispered. The bubbles were all gone now.

Pim closed her eyes. Her wings rested softly on her back. Her smoke made one small, quiet ring.

Goodnight, little dragon. Goodnight, moss. Goodnight, sky.

final.title: Pim and the Wobbly Wings
final.text:
Once upon a time, in a mossy valley, there lived a little dragon named Pim. Pim was small and green, with smoky puffs for breath and tiny wings like wet paper fans. Her scales were the color of new leaves, and they felt cool and smooth, like a pond stone.

Every morning, the big dragons soared over the hills. Whoosh! Whoosh! Their wings made the tall grass bend and sway. Their shadows raced across the meadow like giant galloping clouds. Pim loved to watch them. She also loved to hide behind her mother's tail when they came too close.

Pim stood on the soft, flat grass at the bottom of the meadow. Her knees wobbled. Her tail curled tight around her toes. Her heart went thump, thump, thump, like a drum in a hurry.

"Flap with me, Pim!" called her cousin Bramble. He was already flapping so fast that his feet lifted off the ground. "Up, up, up!" Then he plopped back down with a squishy thump. "See? Easy!"

Pim peeked up at the sky. It looked very big and very far away. A single cloud sailed by, fluffy and slow. "I can't," she whispered. "My wings are too little. And the sky is too high."

So Pim tried a different way. She hopped onto a flat stone and flapped. Flap, flap, flap. Nothing happened but a tiny puff of smoke that smelled like toasted marshmallows.

Puff! Pop! A bubble of smoke floated up and bumped her nose. Pim giggled. The bubble wobbled away over the grass, shining pink and gold in the sun.

Pim watched it drift. It rose, and rose, and then it floated gently down again, as if it were tired and wanted to rest on the clover.

"Bubbles don't mind being light," Pim said slowly. "They just let the breeze carry them. Maybe I could be light, too."

She took a deep breath. She spread her wings wide and let the warm breeze lift her, just a little, like a leaf. Her belly tickled. Her toes lifted off the stone. Pim wobbled, then steadied, and drifted down onto the soft moss.

"Again!" said Bramble, bouncing up and down like a grasshopper.

Pim tried again. Up went one paw. Down went one paw. She swooped, she wobbled, and she landed with a soft thump on her bottom. "Oof!" said Pim. Bramble laughed so hard that a tiny puff of smoke came out of his ears. Pop! Pop!

"Wibble-wobble," sang Pim, and she flapped in a wobbly circle. Bramble flapped too, and together they went wibble-wobble across the clover until they both tumbled into a giggling heap.

Pim lay on her back and looked up. The clouds drifted past like slow white sheep. Maybe the sky wasn't so far away after all.

The sun slid low behind the hills. The sky turned peach and then lavender. The big dragons came home, their wings folded like sleepy umbrellas. One of them winked at Pim as she passed.

Pim sat on the moss beside her cousin. Her wings felt tired and warm. "Tomorrow," she yawned, "I'll try a little higher."

Bramble curled up beside her. The grass whispered. The bubbles were all gone now, but the breeze still smelled of marshmallows.

Pim closed her eyes. Her wings rested softly on her back. Her smoke made one small, quiet ring.

Goodnight, little dragon. Goodnight, moss. Goodnight, sky.

first_draft.title: The Midnight Vegetable Dance
first_draft.text:
At midnight, when the kitchen clock gave its tiny tick and the fridge hummed like a sleepy bumblebee, the vegetables began to whisper. Pip the carrot was the first to wiggle out of the crisper drawer. "Shh," said Mrs. Leek, rustling her green skirts. "Tonight is the night."

The Party Committee had planned everything. There were cucumber balloons, a fizzy lemonade made from a dribble of fizz, and a dance floor of cool, shiny tiles. A bowl of peas rolled across the shelf like marbles. Sir Broccoli had brushed his tiny trees until they sparkled. The celery stalks went crick, crack, crunch as they practised their stomping dance.

But there was a problem. Oona the onion, who was in charge of the music, had lost her spoon. Without a spoon she could not tap the rhythm on the jam jar, and without a rhythm nobody could dance. "Boing-boing!" wailed the springy green beans. "No spoon, no sound, no party at all!"

Tansy the tomato squished her cheeks in thought. "Let's search," she said. "Everyone, quiet as a whisper."

So the vegetables tiptoed. Pip the carrot peeked behind the milk carton. Rumi the radish checked under the butter dish. Zuri the zucchini slid along the top shelf, her long body rolling like a green rope. Nobody found the spoon. Mrs. Leek sighed a sigh that smelled of soil and rain. "Maybe we should just hum," she said.

"Hum?" squeaked Pip. "Hum is boring!"

Then Oona had an idea. She began to tap the lid of the pickle jar with her fingernail. Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. It was small and bright, a clicking sound like a clock with a secret. The peas bounced to it. The celery stomped to it. Even Sir Broccoli wiggled his tiny trees in time.

"Wait," said Zuri, pointing one long finger toward the door. "What's that tapping?"

It was Mr. Ladle, who lived in the drawer by the sink, tapping back with his handle. He had been listening all along. "A party needs a drummer," he said with a clang, "and I'm very good at knocking." So the vegetables danced until their stalks went wobbly and their leaves went floppy. They waltzed around the butter, cha-cha-ed past the yoghurt pots, and spun in one great green swirl.

At last the clock struck one, soft as a feather on a pillow. The party was getting quieter. Pip yawned a yawn as orange as a sunset. "Let's clean up," said Tansy gently, and the vegetables tucked the peas back into their bowl and rolled the balloons into the crisper.

Mr. Ladle hung up his handle. Oona curled her onion layers close and whispered, "Goodnight, fridge." The hum went low and slow, like a cat purring in a warm lap.

Pip settled beside Rumi on a soft bed of lettuce. Mrs. Leek folded her skirts. The cold light glowed blue, and then it dimmed. Outside, the moon was a silver coin. Inside, the vegetables breathed in and out, in and out, until the whole kitchen was still.

Shh. Goodnight, little carrots. Goodnight, sleepy peas.

first_draft.title: Marmalade and the Missing Bell
first_draft.text:
The lighthouse keeper's cat, Marmalade, had lost her bell.

It was a small brass bell, no bigger than a plum, and it had gone jingle-jingle every time she padded across the kitchen floor. Now the kitchen was quiet. Too quiet. Marmalade crept under the table, and the bell did not ring. She crept behind the teapot, and still nothing rang.

Horatio, who was seven and very good at looking, knelt on the rug. "Where did you last hear it?" he asked.

Marmalade blinked slowly. She was not a cat who explained things.

So Horatio thought. He thought about the stairs, which creaked. He thought about the window seat, which was full of cushions. He thought about the washing basket, which smelled of lavender and sea salt.

"Let's go one step at a time," he said.

First they checked the stairs. Each step gave a different sound, creak, squeak, and a long low groan. Horatio counted them out loud. Marmalade sat on the fourth step and licked her paw. No bell.

Next they checked the window seat. Horatio lifted every cushion. Under the blue one he found a button, a dried-up pencil, and one striped sock that did not belong to anybody. No bell.

Then Marmalade stopped in the doorway. Her ears swivelled. From somewhere far above came a faint sound. Tink. Tink. Tink.

"The attic!" Horatio whispered.

The attic ladder was steep and the attic was dusty. Horatio climbed up slowly, one rung at a time, holding on tight. Marmalade padded up behind him, her tail held high like a question mark.

Under an old wooden trunk sat a bundle of wool, and inside the wool, curled up asleep, was a fat grey mouse. Around the mouse's neck, tied with a loop of red thread, hung the bell. Every time the mouse breathed, the bell went tink.

"Well," said Horatio, trying not to laugh. "You borrowed the wrong thing."

The mouse opened one eye. Then the other. Then she yawned, a tiny pink yawn, and that was the end of her being in trouble. Horatio untied the thread with his careful fingers, and the mouse scurried off into a hole behind the trunk, leaving the bell in his palm.

He carried it down the ladder, one rung at a time. In the kitchen, he set it on the table. Marmalade reached up and gave it a gentle tap with her nose. Tink.

She purred so loudly that the teapot seemed to hum along.

Outside, the sea rolled slowly against the rocks. The lighthouse beam swept over the water, round and gold, then dark, then gold again. Horatio yawned. Marmalade curled up in the warm patch by the stove, her bell resting on her paws.

The kettle ticked as it cooled. The clock said goodnight in its soft, slow voice. Tick. Tock. Tink.

Horatio pulled the blanket up to his chin and closed his eyes.

And the lighthouse kept its quiet watch over the sleeping sea.

first_draft.title: Gorble and the Bubble Pancakes
first_draft.text:
Under the big oak tree at the bottom of Pickle Lane lived a monster named Gorble, and Gorble was very, very hungry.

Every night, a rumbling rose from the hollow beneath the roots. Rumble, grumble, gurgle. Tilda, who was seven and a half and had a gap in her front teeth, pressed her nose to the window and listened hard.

"Gorble wants something," she whispered to her cat, Figgy, who did not look worried at all.

The next morning, Tilda crept down the garden path with a tin of paper bubbles and a bag of her grandmother's flour. Gorble's head poked out of the hollow. He had mossy ears, round yellow eyes, and a nose that sniffed like a bellows.

"Pancakes?" he said, in a voice like a wet bathtub. "I smell pancakes. I want pancakes. Or bubbles. Bubbles are very good."

"I don't have pancakes yet," said Tilda. "But I can make some, if you help me stir."

Gorble clapped his mossy hands. The sound was a loud, squelchy *splat-splat*, and a family of sparrows flew off the fence in a fright.

They tried to make the batter in Gorble's hollow. First, they added flour. Gorble sneezed, and the flour went up like a snowstorm and settled on Figgy's whiskers. Figgy looked very cross about it.

Next, they added milk. Gorble slurped the whole jug in one gulp, then burped a bubble as big as a melon. It popped with a noise like a tiny trumpet, and everybody giggled.

"We need something to make it fluffy," said Tilda, frowning at the bowl. "Something light."

Gorble thought very hard. His ears wiggled. Then he said, "Bubbles! I have a hundred of them in my tummy from last winter."

Tilda laughed so hard she had to sit down on a root. "Gorble, you can't keep bubbles in your tummy."

"I can," said Gorble, a little hurt. "Watch."

He opened his wide mouth, and out came a shimmering cloud of silver bubbles. They drifted over the garden, bumping gently into the washing line and the cabbages, and they dropped right into the batter. Tilda stirred and stirred until the mixture was light and frothy.

The pancakes sizzled in the old iron pan over a small, safe fire that Tilda's grandmother had lit in the outdoor stove. They were lumpy and golden and smelled of honey.

Gorble ate eleven of them. Then he ate one more, very slowly, and closed his yellow eyes.

"Tilda," he murmured, "that was the best thing I have ever eaten. Better than moths. Better than socks."

"Socks are not food," said Tilda, yawning.

"Not for everyone," said Gorble, and his belly gave a soft, happy rumble, like a cart rolling far away.

The moon came up over Pickle Lane. The oak leaves hushed. Figgy curled into a warm ball on the step, and the last silver bubble drifted up, up, and vanished into the dark.

Tilda tiptoed home, her pockets full of flour. Behind her, the hollow was quiet.

Gorble was full. Gorble was sleepy.

And the garden was still.

first_draft.title: Octavia and the Lost Spectacles
first_draft.text:
The floorboards creaked at the top of the stairs, one long groan and then another, like an old man stretching after a nap. Ethan pulled his blanket up to his nose and listened. The candle on his windowsill flickered, though nobody had opened a window.

"Just the house settling," he whispered to himself. Houses did that. Everybody knew houses did that.

Then something drifted across the hallway. It was grey and wispy, the shape of a tall person wrapped in a sheet that had been washed too many times. It hummed a tune that went up and down like a kite on a windy day.

Ethan's heart thumped. He sat up. The figure stopped outside his door and gave a small, polite cough.

"Excuse me," said a voice, thin as tissue paper. "I seem to have lost my reading spectacles. I was looking for them everywhere. Under the stairs, behind the coats, inside the biscuit tin. I can't find them anywhere."

Ethan blinked. A ghost with a lost pair of glasses? That was not what ghosts were supposed to do.

"Are you a ghost?" he asked, very carefully.

"Oh, yes. Named Octavia, though nobody has called me that in a hundred years. I used to live in this house, you see, back when it had a lot more chimneys and a lot fewer squeaks."

The candle flame bent low, then straightened, as if it were thinking too.

Ethan slid out of bed and padded across the cold floor. Floorboard number seven gave a loud, squeaky "eek!" under his foot, and Octavia jumped so high her sheet rustled like a bag of crisps.

"Sorry," Ethan giggled. "That one always does that."

"Well, it startled me terribly," said Octavia, dabbing at nothing with a transparent handkerchief.

Together they searched. They peered under the rug. They checked the bookshelf. Ethan looked behind the curtains, where the moon made silver stripes on the wallpaper. At last he spotted a small, round glint near the edge of the bathroom mat, sitting right beside the cat's water bowl.

"Got them!" he cried.

Octavia drifted closer, her misty hands clasped with joy. Her spectacles were tiny and golden, and they fitted perfectly on her nose, though she had to peer over them with a wobble.

"Now I can read the bedtime stories again," she sighed happily. "I've been reading the same page for a century."

Ethan yawned, a huge, wide yawn that made his jaw click.

"Goodnight, Ethan," said Octavia softly. "Keep an eye on floorboard seven."

She floated back into the hall. The humming started again, slow and sleepy, and the house gave one last gentle creak, like a door being closed for the night.

Ethan tucked himself under his blanket. The candle glowed soft and steady. Somewhere below, a kettle began to hum.

The stairs were quiet now. The house was settling. And Ethan was too.

first_draft.title: Sir Florentine and the Feathered Plume
first_draft.text:
On the morning of the Summer Contest, Sir Florentine polished his helmet until it shone like a spoon. Clank went his boots on the castle stones. Tonk went his wooden sword against the practice post. He liked practicing alone, but this morning he hoped someone would join him.

"Good morning, Florentine!" called Dame Saffron, marching across the courtyard. Her red plume bobbed on her helmet like a happy bird. "Shall we have a friendly bout before the contest? Just for fun."

"Just for fun," said Florentine, and his knees wobbled a little. "Gently, mind. My shield is heavier than it looks."

"Gently," promised Saffron, and she tapped his shield. Tok, tok, tok! It sounded like a woodpecker in a hurry.

Florentine tried a clever trick. He ducked low, spun around, and tapped her elbow with his sword. Tonk! Saffron gasped, then laughed so hard that three geese fled into the herb garden, honking in alarm.

"A sneaky move, Sir Florentine!" she said. "Now watch this."

She lunged. He stepped aside. She lunged again, and this time her plume flew straight off her helmet. Whoosh! The wind carried it up, over the wall, and down, down, down into the duck pond with a soft plip.

"My plume!" cried Saffron. "Grandmother sewed that plume herself, stitch by stitch."

They ran to the pond. The water was shallow and brown, and frogs sat on lily pads like tiny green kings. The plume floated among the reeds, its red tips bobbing just out of reach.

Saffron stretched her long sword toward it. Splosh! The tip only made the plume spin in a slow circle. Florentine tried reaching with his hand, but his metal sleeve was too big and too slippery. His arm sank into the mud up to the elbow.

"Squelch," said the mud.

Saffron giggled so hard she had to sit down on the bank, and Florentine began to giggle too, which made the mud squelch again.

When the giggles finally faded, Florentine pulled his arm out, shook off the mud, and stared at the reeds. Then he had an idea. He lay flat on the warm grass, set his shield beside him, and slid his wooden sword across the water. Carefully, carefully, he hooked the very tip of the plume's stem.

Lift, he thought. Gently.

The plume rose, wobbled, and dropped back again. A duck named Mabel waddled over to see what all the fuss was about. She gave the plume a curious peck, and Florentine held his breath. On his third try, he lifted it out of the water and into the sunshine, dripping and proud.

"You did it!" Saffron clapped her muddy hands. She was not cross, not even a little. "Next time, I'll bring a feather to tap your shield."

"And I'll bring a bigger shield," said Florentine, and they laughed until Mabel quacked at them both.

They hung the plume on the windowsill to dry in the sun. Saffron declared the bout a draw. Florentine agreed it was the finest draw in the whole castle.

Evening came softly. The courtyard turned from gold to grey, and the lanterns blinked on one by one. Florentine's shield rested on its hook, dented but happy. The plume dried on the sill, its red tips catching the last of the light. Somewhere an owl said hoo, hoo, and the frogs began their slow, sleepy song.

Florentine yawned. His helmet cooled in the breeze, and his boots stood still by the door.

"Goodnight, shield," he whispered. "Goodnight, sword. Goodnight, castle."

And one by one, the little stars came out to keep watch.

request: Maya is starting at a new school on Monday and she's nervous about making friends

first_draft.title: Maya and the Blue Crayon Sea
first_draft.text:
Maya's new shoes squeaked on the shiny hallway floor. Squeak, squeak, squeak. Her tummy felt like a jar of wobbly jelly.

"Hello, I'm Maya," she whispered, practicing. "Hello, I'm Maya." The classroom smelled of crayons and damp paper. Ms. Lindqvist smiled. "Good morning, Maya. Sit wherever you like."

Maya looked around. Dmitri and Ulla were giggling over a book about penguins. Two girls were stacking blocks. Clack, clack, clack. Everyone already seemed to know each other.

Maya took one step toward the blocks. Then another. Then she sat down by the bookshelf instead, where nobody could see her wobbly tummy.

At playtime, the bell went ding-a-ling! Everyone ran to the big field. Maya ran too, but she ran at the very back. "Can I play?" she called. Her voice came out as small as a mouse.

The children were already chasing a ball. Nobody looked back. Maya's shoes went squeak, squeak, all the way to the fence, and she stood very still.

At lunch, the cafeteria was loud. Clatter, chatter, clink. Every table was full of elbows and giggles. Maya carried her tray to the window seat and ate her sandwich slowly. Crunch. Crunch. Crunch. It did not taste like much.

At the next table, a girl with dark curly hair stared into her empty pencil case. "No blue," she sighed. "How can I finish the sea without blue?"

Maya's hand slipped into her pocket. Her fish-shaped blue crayon was there, smooth and a little warm from her fingers. She held it for a long moment. Then she stood up.

"I have blue," Maya said. Her voice wobbled, but the words came out. She slid the crayon across the table.

The girl's eyes lit up like lanterns. "Thank you! I'm Priya. Is that a fish? It's a splendid fish!"

"Her name is Fishy Fred," Maya said, and Priya laughed a bubbly laugh.

Priya drew waves. Maya drew a frog on a lily pad. "Frogs don't like waves," Priya said. "They like puddles." "Then this frog will swim in a puddle of sea," said Maya, and they both giggled.

Dmitri wandered over with a yellow crayon. "Can I draw the sun?" he asked. "Yes," said Priya. "Right in the corner." Ulla came next, holding her penguin book. "Penguins live in the sea too," she said. "Pull up a chair."

Now the sea had a sun, a fish named Fred, a frog on a lily pad, and three penguins with very round tummies. Swish, swish, went the crayons. Scribble, scribble, went the pencils.

When the bell rang for home, Ms. Lindqvist looked at the big paper and clapped. "What a wonderful sea," she said. Maya's tummy went still, like jelly set in the fridge.

That night, Maya's squeaky shoes sat quietly by the door. Her mum read one page about a sleepy owl, then another. The lamp glowed soft and yellow.

Maya whispered, "Hello, Priya. Hello, Dmitri. Hello, Ulla." Her eyelids grew heavy. Outside, the moon peeked over the rooftops. Hush, hush, went the night.

Goodnight, Maya. Goodnight, Fred. Goodnight, sea.

request: Our old dog Biscuit died last week and Sam misses him a lot

first_draft.title: Biscuit's Tin of Memories
first_draft.text:
Sam found the blue ball under the porch on a wet Tuesday morning. Its rubber had gone soft and grey at the edges, and it was covered in tiny tooth marks, like lopsided little moons. It was Biscuit's ball.

Sam held it tight in both hands. Biscuit had died last week. He was fourteen years old, with frosty whiskers and a wobbly back leg, and his heart had grown too tired to keep going. Mum said it was nobody's fault, and Sam believed her. Mostly. But the house still felt too quiet. Nobody's tail thumped the floorboards at breakfast. Nobody's nose pushed the back door open with a snuffly hello.

"I don't want to put it away," Sam told the kitchen. "But I don't want to lose it either."

Mum was stirring porridge with a wooden spoon. She set it down and sat beside him. "Biscuit would want you to keep his things," she said. "Especially the ones he chewed."

Sam nodded. He had an idea, but it was a big, messy one. It needed a friend.

Priya lived next door. She was eight like him, and she had a loud laugh and a rope ladder up her tree house. Sam pulled on his wellies and splashed across the wet grass. Splish, splosh, squelch. Priya was kneeling by her vegetable patch, pulling up carrots as if they might escape.

"I'm making a Biscuit tin," Sam said. "For memories. Will you help?"

"Yes," said Priya, already wiping mud on her jeans. "What goes in it?"

That was the tricky part. Sam tried to think of one thing, and every thing seemed wrong. A photo felt flat. A bone felt silly. Then he remembered the morning Biscuit had snatched a sausage roll off the picnic table and sneezed crumbs all over Grandma's hat.

Sam giggled. Then he stopped. Then he giggled again, and the giggle wobbled in the middle like jelly.

Priya didn't say anything. She just picked up a flat grey stone and handed it to him.

"That one's the sausage roll," Sam said.

They hunted for more. Priya found a heart-shaped pebble for the afternoon Biscuit had sat on her feet for an entire hour, so she couldn't move. Sam found a smooth white stone for the squeaky duck Biscuit had carried round the garden like a prize. They drew on the stones with Priya's purple marker, though Sam's duck came out looking more like a potato with feet.

Back at Sam's house, they found Mum's old biscuit tin with the blue lid. They dropped the stones in one by one. Clink. Clink. Clatter. Then Sam pushed the ball in too, but it stuck halfway, and the lid wouldn't close. He pushed harder. Priya giggled. The ball popped out and rolled across the floor, right up to Mum's slippers.

Mum picked it up and looked at it for a long moment. Her eyes were shiny.

"Maybe the ball can keep the tin company," she said softly, "on the windowsill, where Biscuit used to watch the birds."

So that is what they did. The tin went on the shelf beside the photo of Biscuit wearing a paper party hat. The ball sat on the windowsill in the last of the evening light.

Later, when the room had gone blue and quiet, Sam stood at the window. He missed Biscuit. He missed him in the morning, and in the afternoon, and at the very end of the day, when the house should have been full of paws. Mum sat beside him and said she missed him too.

"Can we still tell him things?" Sam asked.

"We can," said Mum. "He'd like that."

So Sam told the dark garden about the sausage roll, and the squeaky duck, and the way Biscuit used to sigh when he was happy. The apple tree leaves whispered back. Sam yawned, a big slow yawn.

Mum tucked the blanket up to his chin. The window glowed soft with moonlight. The blue ball sat quietly on the sill, the tin sat quietly on the shelf, and the house settled down around them, slow and warm.

Goodnight, Sam. Goodnight, Biscuit.

first_draft.title: Gideon and the Mossy Pillow
first_draft.text:
Far above the sleeping meadow, an owl named Gideon blinked his big round eyes. Then he yawned. It was a long, slow yawn, the kind that makes your whole face wobble.

"Hoo," said Gideon softly. "Hoo, hoo. It is time for bed."

But his old oak hollow was full of crunchy leaves, and every leaf rustled when he settled down. Shh, rustle. Shh, rustle. Gideon sighed and flapped out into the moonlight.

He landed on the fence post. The wood was cold, and the wind whistled through the wire. "Too chilly," he murmured. His feathers puffed up like a dandelion clock.

He tried the haystack next. It was warm, but it scratched his tummy, and a sleepy hen clucked from below. "Hush, hush, not here," she said. Gideon yawned and drifted on, wobbling on the breeze.

At the edge of the pond sat a small brown hedgehog named Matilda, snuffling in the reeds. She looked up with a twitch of her nose.

"You look like a sleepy cloud," she said.

"I need a soft place to rest," said Gideon. "Something warm, but not scratchy, and not too wet."

Matilda thought for a long moment. Then she trundled into a thick bank of moss beside the water. "Here," she said. "This moss is soft as a pillow. I sleep here every night."

Gideon hopped in and wiggled. Squish, fluff. Squish, fluff. The moss hugged him like a blanket. He tucked his head under one wing.

"Hoo," he whispered. "Hoo, hoo. The night is blue."

Matilda curled into a round, prickly ball beside him. The pond lapped softly against the reeds. Lap, hush. Lap, hush.

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Humming Crystal Cave
first_draft.text:
Zoe found the cave on the last warm afternoon of summer, hidden behind a curtain of ivy at the bottom of Thimble Hill. Her tortoise, Pebble, came along too, though he took his time about it.

"Wait for me!" Zoe called, pushing through the leaves. Pebble followed one slow step at a time. Scritch. Scratch. Scritch. His shell bumped against the stones like a tiny drum.

Inside, the air smelled of cold rain and old, sleepy stone. Zoe clicked on her torch. The beam wobbled across damp walls, then caught something that made her gasp.

Crystals! Hundreds of them, pale as milk and sharp as icicles, poked out of the walls and ceiling. In the very middle of the cave stood one enormous crystal, purple as a plum, glowing softly like a lamp someone had left on just for her.

"Oh, Pebble," Zoe whispered. "Look."

Pebble looked. Then he yawned, very slowly, and tucked his head into his shell.

Zoe crept closer. The crystal was cool and smooth under her fingertips, and when she tilted her torch, tiny rainbows danced across the walls. Then she heard it: a low hum, like a bee singing inside a jar.

"I just want a tiny piece to keep," Zoe said. She picked a chip of crystal from the floor, no bigger than a button, and slid it into her pocket. Then the hum grew louder. Somewhere high above, stones began to rattle.

Rumble. Clatter. Crash. A shower of gravel rained down, and when the dust settled, the way they had come in was gone. A heap of rocks stood where the ivy gap had been, and only a thin line of daylight leaked through the top.

Zoe's heart went thump, thump, thump. She wanted to shout for Mum. Instead, she shoved at the nearest rock. It didn't budge. She pushed harder, and two more rocks slid down, and she jumped back. "Oh no," she said in a small voice.

Pebble, who had been watching everything with his calm, round eyes, did not hurry at all. He just sat still. Zoe took a deep breath. Her grandad always said, "When things go wrong, slow hands and clever eyes will find the way." She had never tried it in a cave before.

So she sat down beside Pebble and looked properly. Not at the big rocks, but at the spaces between them. Here was a small gap, shaped like a letter V. There was a flat stone that might lift. And at the very top, a crack where the daylight came through.

Zoe lifted the flat stone with both hands and set it gently aside. Then she moved the next one, and the next, one at a time. Each time a stone rolled, she waited for the dust to settle before she moved another. Her arms ached. Her knees turned dusty. But the gap grew wider.

At last, a patch of green light fell across the floor. Pebble lifted his head. "Yes, that's the way out," Zoe said. "Come on, slow and steady." Pebble walked through the gap, scrape, scrape, the way he did everything, and Zoe squeezed through right behind him.

Outside, the sun was warm on her face. Mum came running up the hill, her cheeks pale, and wrapped Zoe in a hug so tight that the crystal chip poked her through her pocket. "You're safe," Mum said. "You're safe." Zoe nodded into her jumper.

Later, at the kitchen table, Zoe pulled out the little chip and turned it in the lamplight. It sparkled gold, then blue. "It was so beautiful in there," she said. "I wanted to keep the whole cave."

Mum smiled. "The cave is still there, Zoe, glowing in the dark, waiting for the next person who looks carefully. That's the best kind of treasure. You look after it, and you leave some of it for others."

Zoe thought about the purple crystal, humming in the quiet, and how it had stayed safe because she had listened and gone slowly. Looking gently, she decided, was better than grabbing. Some of the most amazing things are the ones we leave exactly where they are.

That night, Zoe placed the crystal chip on her windowsill, where it caught the moonlight. Pebble snuffled in his box by the bed. The house creaked softly, the way houses do when they are settling down. The hum of the cave was only a memory now, a far-off bee in a far-off jar.

Zoe pulled up her blanket. Her eyes grew heavy. Her breathing slowed, long and soft.

Goodnight, Pebble. Goodnight, crystals.

Sleep now, slow and steady.
